scenes.heading: The colours of a chessboard
scenes.title: The colours of a chessboard
scenes.narration: A chessboard may look like a collection of little squares. Its colours can reveal something numbers alone cannot: whether a covering is impossible.

scenes.heading: What a domino uses
scenes.title: What a domino uses
scenes.narration: In AMC, you may need to spot an odd or even pattern. In a Rossmoyne style problem, explain why every allowed piece follows the same rule. A MAWA investigation might explore which boards can be tiled. Let us move from pairs to colouring.

scenes.heading: Count the squares
scenes.title: Count the squares
scenes.narration: Start with a three by three chessboard. The top-left square is blue and the colours alternate. Count each colour. Is the number of squares odd or even?

scenes.heading: Pair the squares
scenes.title: Pair the squares
scenes.narration: There are five blue squares and four gold squares, nine altogether. They cannot all be grouped into pairs: one square remains.

scenes.heading: Cross out the leftmost pair
scenes.title: Cross out the leftmost pair
scenes.narration: Take a full four by four board. In the top row, cross out the two squares farthest to the left. One is blue and one is gold. Can dominoes cover the rest? Each domino covers two squares sharing an edge.

scenes.heading: A seven-domino covering
scenes.title: A seven-domino covering
scenes.narration: Yes. Place one domino across the remaining two squares in the top row. Then place two horizontal dominoes across each of the three lower rows. That is seven dominoes, covering fourteen squares.

scenes.heading: Remove opposite corners
scenes.title: Remove opposite corners
scenes.narration: Here is a harder puzzle. A four by four board has its top-left and bottom-right corners removed. Each domino covers two squares sharing an edge. The challenge is to cover the remaining board with seven dominoes and no overlap. Is that possible?

scenes.heading: Count each colour
scenes.title: Count each colour
scenes.narration: Colour the full board like a chessboard. There are eight blue squares and eight gold squares. Each domino, horizontal or vertical, covers one of each colour.

scenes.heading: Six blue and eight gold
scenes.title: Six blue and eight gold
scenes.narration: The two removed corners are both blue. That leaves six blue and eight gold squares. Seven dominoes would need seven of each colour. Since only six blue squares remain, the covering is impossible.

scenes.heading: When counts agree
scenes.title: When counts agree
scenes.narration: It is a mistake to stop at fourteen squares. Fourteen is divisible by two, but the colours do not balance. And colour balance alone does not guarantee a covering: the squares must still join up legally.

scenes.heading: Build or rule out a covering
scenes.title: Build or rule out a covering
scenes.narration: In an exam, identify what every allowed piece does. Pick a colouring that reveals the pattern. Count the colours and write a clear reason, not just an answer.
